name: Dnyaneshwar
role: 13th-century Marathi saint-poet, author of the Dnyaneshwari
summary: Dnyaneshwar was a 13th-century Marathi saint who explained the Bhagavad Gita in everyday Marathi at about 16 and is remembered at Alandi.
about: Dnyaneshwar, also called Mauli, was a Marathi saint-poet of the 13th century. Tradition says he was born in 1275 near Paithan to a family excluded by local Brahmins, and that he and his siblings Nivruttinath, Sopan and Muktabai grew up in the Nath tradition. His Dnyaneshwari, written around 1290 in Marathi, is a famous commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, and the Amrutanubhav is his independent work. Legends tell of a talking buffalo and a moving wall. Tradition says he entered a living samadhi at Alandi in 1296, aged about 21. Each year, palanquins with his sandals walk from Alandi to Pandharpur in the Wari.
kidSummary: Dnyaneshwar was a young saint from Maharashtra who explained the Bhagavad Gita in simple Marathi when he was only about sixteen. Stories tell that he once rode a moving wall. Every year, pilgrims carry his sandals in a palanquin on a long walk to Pandharpur.

story.title: A family left out
story.text: Dnyaneshwar's family was shut out by their neighbours because of an old rule, but the four children, three brothers and a sister, stayed close.

story.title: Learning from a guru
story.text: His elder brother Nivruttinath became his teacher in the Nath tradition and helped him grow in wisdom.

story.title: The Gita in Marathi
story.text: Around the age of sixteen, he is said to have told the meaning of the Bhagavad Gita in plain Marathi so that everyone could understand.

story.title: The moving wall
story.text: One legend says a yogi arrived on a tiger, so Dnyaneshwar sat on a wall and made it glide forward, and the yogi bowed.

story.title: Samadhi at Alandi
story.text: In 1296, tradition says, he entered a samadhi at Alandi by the Indrayani river, and devotees still honour him there.

story.title: The Wari
story.text: Today, every year, a palanquin carrying his sandals leaves Alandi and walks about 21 days with thousands of singing pilgrims to Pandharpur.

teaches: Great ideas should be shared in a language everyone knows
Siblings and friends make a family strong

facts.text: He is said to have completed the Dnyaneshwari, a commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, around 1290, when he was only about 16.
Some legends say that when Brahmins mocked him, he put his hand on a buffalo's forehead and the animal recited a Vedic verse, after he argued that the Vedas call all life sacred.
In a famous legend, the yogi Changdev rode a tiger, and Dnyaneshwar answered by making a wall move like a vehicle.
He is said to have entered sanjeevan samadhi at Alandi in 1296, aged about 21, and devotees still regard him as alive there.
His symbolic sandals (paduka) travel by palanquin from Alandi to Pandharpur, a walk of roughly 21 days and about 250 kilometres.
In the Dnyaneshwari he compares an ideal doer of duty to the Sun, which seems to rise and set but never actually moves, so that such a person seems to act yet stays unattached.
The Dnyaneshwari ends with the Pasaydan (spelt Pasaayadana on Wikipedia), a closing prayer in which he asks nothing for himself and seeks the good of everyone in the world.
According to tradition, when Namdev prayed to Vithoba after Dnyaneshwar's samadhi, Dnyaneshwar was brought back to life to meet his friend.
Muktabai's poem 'Tatiche Abhang', the Song of the Door, asks her brother Dnyaneshwar to open the door and teaches that a wise person stays cool as water even when the world is hot with anger.
Tradition says the scribe Sachchidananda, whom Dnyaneshwar is said to have brought back to life, wrote down the Dnyaneshwari as the young saint spoke it.
Scholar Bhagwat ranks Dnyaneshwar's place in Marathi literature alongside the place Dante holds in Italian literature.
The Dnyaneshwari and the Amrutanubhav are the oldest surviving literary works in the Marathi language.
When the family travelled to Nashik, a tiger crossed their path and Nivruttinath got separated and hid in a cave, where he met the yogi Gahaninath, who taught him the Nath way.
The yogi Changdev once sent the siblings a blank note as a test; Dnyaneshwar replied with 65 verses, later called the Changdev Pasashti, that sum up the heart of Vedanta.
The tiger-riding yogi Changdev is said to have ended up as a disciple of Dnyaneshwar's sister Muktabai.
Popular belief says the yogi Changdev lived for 1,400 years, and a village named after him near Muktainagar has an old temple linked to him.
In the Amrutanubhav he asks whether an eye can see itself, the sky can enter itself or a fire can burn itself, to show that pure awareness cannot be turned into an object.
In the traditional account, Nivruttinath, Dnyaneshwar, Sopan and Muktabai were born about two years apart, in 1273, 1275, 1277 and 1279.
Because their father had returned to family life after becoming a renunciate, local Brahmins refused the brothers the sacred thread ceremony and shut the family out of village life.
He wrote the Dnyaneshwari in everyday Marathi rather than Sanskrit, so that people who did not know the priests' language could understand the Gita.
